summary: אָדוֹן is a lord: the one a servant belongs to and obeys, and so a slave’s master, a wife’s husband, the ruler of a house or a land, and, as אֲדֹנִי “my lord”, the courteous word to anyone a speaker sets above himself, man or angel. Its opposite is עֶבֶד, servant, and Malachi 1:6 gives what is owed to it: a servant honours his master. Yahweh is הָאָדוֹן, lord of all the earth and lord of lords, and the form אֲדֹנָי, about 440 times, is kept for him alone, most often in prayer and in the prophets’ אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה. Psalm 110:1 has both in one line: Yahweh speaks to one whom David calls אֲדֹנִי, “my lord”, the form said to men, and the New Testament names him as Jesus, made lord by God. Ugaritic and Phoenician have the same word for lord, father and master. אֶדֶן is the socket or base a frame or pillar stands in; no verse or cognate yet shows how it comes from the same root.

words.summary: About 780 times: some 340 as אָדוֹן of men, angels and God, and about 440 in the form אֲדֹנָי, said of God only. With “my” the singular is used, אֲדֹנִי “my lord” (195 times, always to a man or an angel). With every other suffix the plural is used even of one master: אֲדֹנָיו is “his master” Abraham (Gen 24:9) or Potiphar (Gen 39:2), with a singular verb (Exo 21:4) or adjective (אֲדֹנִים קָשֶׁה, “a hard lord”, Isa 19:4). It is a plural of rank, as אֱלֹהִים is, and a real plural only where the context has several lords (Deu 10:17; Isa 26:13; Jer 27:4). אֲדֹנָי is that plural with “my”, pointed with a long ā where the address to men has a short one (אֲדֹנַי, “my lords”, Gen 19:2). Scripture’s Aramaic does not use this word: Daniel has מָרֵא (Dan 2:47; 5:23) and the Peshitta מָרָא, מָריָא, of another root.

senses.gloss: master of a servant or slave
senses.definition: The one a servant or slave belongs to, works for and obeys. The pair עֶבֶד and אָדוֹן define each other: the servant honours his master, looks to his hand, and is free of him only by release or in the grave.

evidence.note: בֵּן יְכַבֵּד אָב וְעֶבֶד אֲדֹנָיו, “a son honours a father, and a servant his master”: what a father is to a son, an אָדוֹן is to a servant, and fear is owed to him.
“As the eyes of servants are to the hand of their masters (אֲדוֹנֵיהֶם), as the eyes of a maid to the hand of her mistress (גְּבִרְתָּהּ).”
The Hebrew slave: his master gives him a wife, and she and her children are her master’s; if he says אָהַבְתִּי אֶת־אֲדֹנִי, “I love my master”, his master pierces his ear and he serves him for good.
The servant puts his hand under the thigh of “Abraham his master” and swears to him.
He prays to “Yahweh, God of my master Abraham”.
Joseph “in the house of his master the Egyptian”.
“You shall not hand over a servant to his master, who has escaped to you from his master.”
In the grave “the servant is free from his master”.
“As with the servant, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress.”
“Do not slander a servant to his master.”

senses.definition: A wife’s husband, as the one she is under. Sarah speaks of Abraham so, and Peter takes her word as her obedience.

evidence.note: Sarah laughs within herself: וַאדֹנִי זָקֵן, “and my lord is old”.
“As Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord (κύριον; Peshitta מָרי, “my lord”)”: Gen 18:12 expounded.
The woman falls at the door of the house “where her lord was”, and “her lord rose in the morning”.
The women of Samaria “who say to their lords, Bring, and let us drink”.
To the king’s bride: “for he is your lord (אֲדֹנַיִךְ); bow down to him.”

senses.gloss: lord of a house, a land or a people; ruler, owner
senses.definition: One set over a household, a land or a people, or owning a property. It stands beside מֹשֵׁל “ruler” and מֶלֶךְ “king”, and a people without one are sheep without a shepherd.

evidence.note: Joseph: God “has set me as a father to Pharaoh and as lord (לְאָדוֹן) to all his house and ruler in all the land of Egypt … God has set me as lord to all Egypt.”
“He set him lord (אָדוֹן) to his house and ruler (מֹשֵׁל) over all his possession.”
“I will shut Egypt up in the hand of a hard lord (אֲדֹנִים קָשֶׁה), and a strong king shall rule over them”: lord and king in parallel, the plural with a singular adjective.
“The man, the lord of the land (אֲדֹנֵי הָאָרֶץ), spoke harshly with us.”
Shemer, אֲדֹנֵי הָהָר, the owner of the hill that Omri bought.
“Yahweh our God, lords (אֲדֹנִים) other than you have ruled over us.”
Israel scattered “as sheep that have no shepherd; and Yahweh said, These have no lord (לֹא־אֲדֹנִים לָאֵלֶּה)”: the king is about to fall.
The boasters: “our lips are with us; who is lord to us?”
The lament for a king: הוֹי אָדוֹן, “Alas, lord!”, which Jehoiakim will not have.
Zedekiah will have it: “they will lament for you, Alas, lord!”
The cupbearer and the baker sinned “against their lord, the king of Egypt”.
Rezon fled “from Hadadezer king of Zobah his lord”.

senses.gloss: my lord: respectful address to a superior
senses.definition: אֲדֹנִי, “my lord”, said to or of anyone the speaker sets above himself: a king, a prophet, a father, an elder brother, a host, a stranger. The speaker is then “your servant” or “your maidservant”, and often bows. It claims no more than respect.

evidence.note: Judah to Joseph: בִּי אֲדֹנִי, “Pardon, my lord, let your servant speak a word in my lord’s ears … for you are as Pharaoh.”
David calls after Saul, אֲדֹנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ, “my lord the king”, and bows with his face to the ground.
The sons of Heth to Abraham, a sojourner among them: “Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God in our midst.”
Rachel to her father: “let it not burn in the eyes of my lord”.
Jacob of his brother: “thus shall you say to my lord, to Esau: thus says your servant Jacob”.
Rebekah to a stranger at the well: “Drink, my lord.”
Aaron to Moses, his younger brother: בִּי אֲדֹנִי.
Joshua: “My lord Moses, restrain them.”
Hannah to Eli the priest: “No, my lord.”
Obadiah falls on his face: “Is it you, my lord Elijah?”
The Shunammite to Elisha: “No, my lord, man of God, do not lie to your maidservant.”
Ruth to Boaz: “Let me find favour in your eyes, my lord.”
“Let your maidservant speak a word to my lord the king.”
Bathsheba bows to the ground: “Let my lord king David live for ever.”

senses.gloss: my lord, said to an angel
senses.definition: The same address with the same pointing, said to an angel: to the commander of Yahweh’s army, to the angel who speaks with Zechariah, to the one who touches Daniel.

evidence.note: “I am commander of the army of Yahweh” … Joshua falls on his face: “What does my lord (אֲדֹנִי) say to his servant?”
Lot to the two angels: הִנֶּה נָּא־אֲדֹנַי, “Look now, my lords”, the plural with a short a.
Gideon to the angel of Yahweh, not yet knowing him: בִּי אֲדֹנִי. Two verses on, when Yahweh has turned to him, the text points אֲדֹנָי (Jdg 6:15).
“What are these, my lord?” And the angel who spoke with me said …
“How can the servant of this my lord speak with this my lord?”
“My lord, what shall be the end of these things?”

senses.gloss: my lord: the king at Yahweh’s right hand
senses.definition: In Psalm 110:1 David calls אֲדֹנִי, “my lord”, one to whom Yahweh speaks and whom Yahweh seats at his right hand until his enemies are subdued. Jesus and the apostles read the verse of the Messiah.

evidence.note: נְאֻם יַהְוֶה לַאדֹנִי שֵׁב לִימִינִי, “the utterance of Yahweh to my lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” The name for the speaker; for the one addressed, the form said to men.
Jesus: “How then does David in spirit call him lord? … If David calls him lord, how is he his son?” The Greek has κύριος twice; the Peshitta keeps two forms, מָריָא למָרי, “the Lord to my lord”.
Peter: David did not ascend into the heavens, but says this; “God has made him both lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.”
“To which of the angels has he ever said, Sit at my right hand …?”
“He must reign until he has put all the enemies under his feet.”

senses.definition: Yahweh as lord: with the article, הָאָדוֹן; as lord of all the earth; as “our Lord”; and as lord of all who are called lords. He claims from Israel what a servant owes a master.

evidence.note: “If I am a lord (אֲדוֹנִים אָנִי), where is my fear? says Yahweh of armies.”
“Yahweh your God, he is God of the gods and Lord of the lords (אֲדֹנֵי הָאֲדֹנִים).”
“Tremble, earth, before the Lord (אָדוֹן), before the God of Jacob”: the two in parallel.
Three times a year every male appears “before the Lord Yahweh” (הָאָדֹן יַהְוֶה); so Exo 34:23.
“The ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth.”
The mountains melt “before Yahweh, before the Lord of all the earth”.
“The utterance of the Lord, Yahweh of armies, the Mighty One of Israel.”
יַהְוֶה אֲדֹנֵינוּ, “Yahweh our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!”
“Yahweh is great, and our Lord is above all gods.”
“This day is holy to our Lord.”
“His Lord will bring his reproach back on him.”
“The Lord (הָאָדוֹן) whom you seek will come suddenly to his temple.”

senses.gloss: אֲדֹנָי: the Lord, said of God only
senses.definition: The form אֲדֹנָי, kept for God. In prayer it is still “my Lord”, the servant’s word to his master; in the prophets and psalms it also stands as a name in the third person, in parallel with Yahweh and with God. Nearly 300 of its 440 uses are the pair אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה, over 200 of them in Ezekiel.

evidence.note: “I said to Yahweh, You are my Lord (אֲדֹנָי אָתָּה)”: the “my” is meant.
אֱלֹהַי וַאדֹנָי, “my God and my Lord”: beside a word that plainly has “my”.
“The Lord (אֲדֹנָי) will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion, and Yahweh will lay bare …”: the two as one subject in parallel lines.
Abraham: “I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, and I am dust and ashes.”
Abram’s first recorded prayer: אֲדֹנָי יַהְוֶה, “Lord Yahweh, what will you give me?”
Moses to Yahweh: בִּי אֲדֹנָי, the same plea as בִּי אֲדֹנִי to a man, with the other pointing, and “your servant” in the same breath.
Gideon, after אֲדֹנִי to the angel in verse 13.
“Lord, hear; Lord, forgive; Lord, attend and act.”
“I pray, Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant.”
“I will thank you, Lord my God, with all my heart.”
“I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up.”
“He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord mocks them.”
In the psalm that says אֲדֹנִי of David’s lord: “the Lord (אֲדֹנָי) at your right hand shatters kings in the day of his anger.”
“The Lord will not cast off for ever.”
“The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom.”
“The Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand.”
“The Lord Yahweh does nothing unless he has revealed his counsel to his servants the prophets … the Lord Yahweh has spoken; who will not prophesy?”
“The spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me, because Yahweh has anointed me.”
Isa 61:1 read by Jesus in Nazareth: πνεῦμα κυρίου, Peshitta רֻוחֵה דּמָריָא.

evidence.locator: PSA 110:1 word 5, לַאדֹנִי → κυρίῳ; GEN 45:8 word 12, לְאָדוֹן → κύριον; MAL 1:6 word 5, אֲדֹנָיו → κύριον; DEU 10:17 words 7–8, אֲדֹנֵי הָאֲדֹנִים → κύριος κυρίων

evidence.note: Psa 110:1 quoted: εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου. Greek has one word for the name and for אֲדֹנִי.
Sarah’s אֲדֹנִי (Gen 18:12): κύριον αὐτὸν καλοῦσα.
“King of those who reign as kings and Lord of those who rule as lords”: Deu 10:17’s title.
“A servant is not above his lord”: the pair עֶבֶד and אָדוֹן in Greek.
“Masters (κύριοι), give your servants what is just, knowing that you also have a master in heaven.”

evidence.locator: ISA 1:24 word 3, הָאָדוֹן → δεσπότης; ISA 3:1 word 3; ISA 10:33 word 2; DAN 9:15 word 2, אֲדֹנָי → δέσποτα

evidence.note: Simeon’s prayer, in the terms of servant and master: “Now you release your servant, δέσποτα.”
The ecclesia’s prayer: “δέσποτα, you are the God who made the heaven and the earth.”
Servants under a yoke are to count their own masters (δεσπότας) worthy of all honour, as Mal 1:6 says a servant does.

parallels.note: Lord of the house and ruler over all it holds.
A hard lord, a strong king.

evidence.note: The blemished offering sacrificed “to the Lord (לַאדֹנָי), for I am a great king”.

parallels.note: Father and lord are honoured alike, by son and by servant; Joseph is both to Pharaoh’s house.
God of gods and Lord of lords; “my God and my Lord”.

evidence.note: “You will answer, Lord my God.”

parallels.note: The mistress, the lord’s counterpart over a maid.

opposites.note: Servant and lord are the two ends of one tie; whoever says “my lord” calls himself “your servant”.

phrases.gloss: pardon, my lord (opening a plea); to God, בִּי אֲדֹנָי

evidence.note: To Yahweh: בִּי אֲדֹנָי.
In the other order: יַהְוֶה אֲדֹנָי חֵילִי, “Yahweh the Lord is my strength”.
The words Ezekiel is sent to say.

phrases.gloss: the utterance of the Lord Yahweh

evidence.note: “The ark of Yahweh, the Lord of all the earth.”
Said of the Lamb: “he is lord of lords and king of kings”.

phrases.gloss: Alas, lord! (the lament for a king)

words.summary: 57 times, 55 of them the cast sockets of the tabernacle; Job and the Song of Songs use it of what the earth and a pillar are founded on. How it comes from the root of אָדוֹן is not clear. A lord is one a house rests on, as a frame rests in its socket, but no verse draws that picture, and no cognate meaning “base” has been found: the Ugaritic and Phoenician words of the root mean “lord, father, master” only, so they count against this word in the tally, and its meaning rests on scripture’s use alone.

senses.gloss: socket of the tabernacle’s frames and pillars
senses.definition: A block of cast metal set on the ground, into which the tenons of a frame or the foot of a pillar went: silver, a talent each, for the frames of the dwelling and the pillars of the veil; bronze for the pillars of the door screen and of the court.

evidence.note: “Forty sockets of silver (אַדְנֵי־כֶסֶף) under the twenty frames: two sockets under one frame for its two tenons.”
“The hundred talents of silver were for casting the sockets of the holy place and the sockets of the veil: a hundred sockets for the hundred talents, a talent to a socket (כִּכָּר לָאָדֶן).”
The veil hangs on four pillars “on four sockets of silver”.
“You shall cast for them five sockets of bronze”, for the pillars of the screen.
The court: “its pillars twenty and their sockets twenty, of bronze”.
Moses set up the dwelling: he put down its sockets first, then set its frames.
The frames, bars, pillars and sockets are the charge of the sons of Merari.

senses.gloss: base that a thing is founded on
senses.definition: What a structure is set on and stands by: the bases of the earth in Yahweh’s question to Job, the gold bases under pillars of marble in the Song.

evidence.note: Of the earth: “On what were its bases (אֲדָנֶיהָ) sunk, or who laid its corner stone?”
“His legs are pillars of marble, founded on bases of fine gold (מְיֻסָּדִים עַל־אַדְנֵי־פָז).”

parallels.note: The earth’s bases and its corner stone are asked after together.
The pillar is what stands on the base; the two are counted together.

cognates.note: The head of a household, whether named as its father or its lord: the range Hebrew has in Gen 45:8, “a father to Pharaoh and lord to all his house”.

evidence.note: Glossed “father (head of household)”; “lord”, and compared with the Hebrew word and with a Ugaritic personal name written a-du-nu in syllabic cuneiform.

cognates.gloss: king; father; master of a slave; gentleman; (of a god) lord
cognates.note: The same spread as the Hebrew: ruler, head of a family, a slave’s owner, a title of respect, and the title of a god (“to the Lord Baal-hammon” in the Carthage dedications).

evidence.note: "[Heb. ʾadōn] n.m. 1. KING", CIS i 89.2/3 ʾdnn, "our king Baalrom"; "2. FATHER", Poen. 1141P, "May you live long, my father!"; "3. SLAVE MASTER", CIS i 4901, "<Dedicated> to the Lady Tinnit-Phanebal and to the Lord Baalhammon is what Safot, a slave owned by his master Milkyaton … vowed"; "4. GENTLEMAN", KAI 119.4/5.

cognates.gloss: Adonay, Adonim: “Lord”, standing for a god’s name
cognates.note: Phoenician also uses the suffixed and plural forms as a divine title in place of a name, in personal names, as Hebrew uses אֲדֹנָי.

evidence.note: "[Heb. ʾadōnay] d. ʾADONAY, var. ʾADONIM (“Lord, God”) … in personal names in place of a divine name": Benz 149 ʿbdʾdny, "Servant of Adoni/Adonay"; Benz 181 šmʾdnm, "Adonim is the Name".

doctrine.statement: Psalm 110:1 reads נְאֻם יַהְוֶה לַאדֹנִי: “the utterance of Yahweh to my lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” Two are in the verse. Yahweh speaks; the one spoken to is another, whom David calls “my lord”, who sits at Yahweh’s right hand and waits while Yahweh subdues his enemies for him. The word is אֲדֹנִי, the form said 195 times in scripture to or of a man or an angel (Sarah of Abraham, Gen 18:12; David to Saul, 1Sa 24:9; Joshua to the commander of Yahweh’s army, Jos 5:14) and nowhere else in the Psalms; the form kept for God, אֲדֹנָי, stands in verse 5 of the same psalm. Jesus asks from this verse how the Christ can be David’s son when David calls him lord (Mat 22:42–45): the one addressed is the Christ, David’s descendant and yet David’s superior. Peter says that David did not ascend into the heavens, that the words are spoken of Jesus, raised and exalted to the right hand of God, and concludes that “God has made him both lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Act 2:32–36): his lordship is given him by God. Hebrews says the words were spoken to the son and to no angel (Heb 1:13), and that after offering one sacrifice he sat down at the right hand of God, waiting until his enemies are made his footstool (Heb 10:12–13). Paul says he must reign until all enemies are under his feet, that the one who put all things under him is plainly excepted, and that the son himself will then be subject to him, that God may be all in all (1Co 15:25–28). So Yahweh and David’s lord are two: one God, the Father, and one lord, Jesus Christ (1Co 8:6), a man of David’s line whom God raised, seated beside himself and made lord, and who remains subject to him.

A servant honours his master, and Yahweh asks, “If I am a lord, where is my fear?” (Mal 1:6). Servants look to their master’s hand, “so our eyes are to Yahweh our God” (Psa 123:2). Those who pray אֲדֹנָי call themselves “your servant” in the same breath (Exo 4:10; Neh 1:11), and Israel confesses that other lords have ruled over them beside him (Isa 26:13). Jesus says that no one can serve two lords (Mat 6:24) and asks, “Why do you call me, Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?” (Luk 6:46). To call God, or his son, lord is to take the place of a servant: the title is owed obedience, and it is empty without it.

Yahweh is God of the gods and Lord of the lords (Deu 10:17; Psa 136:3), and the Lord of all the earth: the ark that went before Israel into the land was his (Jos 3:11, 13), the mountains melt before him (Psa 97:5), and the wealth of the nations is to be devoted to him when the daughter of Zion threshes many peoples (Mic 4:13). Every other lord, of a house or of a kingdom, holds his place under this one, as Joseph says God set him lord of Egypt (Gen 45:8–9).

note:
Root: אדנ, the key BDB files the words under and the root the database gives the tokens of אָדוֹן; no other entry has it.

אֲדֹנָי is treated as senses of אָדוֹן (id `adonai`), not as a word of its own, because BDB has one key (a.be.ac) for both and a key can be on one word only; a separate word would have no uses counted. It has no name entry either: TIPNR’s Deity record (LORD@Gen.1.1) is tagged on names/yahweh.json by Yahweh’s own BDB keys, and the God-words of elah.json are likewise words, not names. Counts are from the pointed text (TAHOT): אֲדֹנָי 438 to 440 tokens (with prefixes; Gen 18:3 included), אֲדֹנָי followed by the name 294 times (Ezekiel 211), the name followed by אֲדֹנָי 6 times, אֲדֹנִי “my lord” 195 times.

For the reviewer: (1) Gen 18:3 אֲדֹנָי (Abraham to the three men) and Gen 19:18 אֲדֹנָי (Lot to the angels) carry the pointing kept for God; they are not cited, since who is addressed is the question the pointing answers. (2) Psa 110:5 אֲדֹנָי עַל־יְמִינְךָ is cited only for the form; whether it is said to the king of Yahweh (as Psa 16:8; 109:31, Yahweh at the right hand of the one he helps) is not argued. (3) Mal 3:1 הָאָדוֹן is cited under the title of Yahweh on the ground that הָאָדוֹן with the article is elsewhere always Yahweh and the temple is “his”; if it is read of the messenger of the covenant, move it. (4) Neh 3:5 (“the work of their lord”) and Ezr 10:3 (“the counsel of אֲדֹנָי”) can be read of God or of a man and are not cited. (5) Rev 17:14 gives “lord of lords” to the Lamb; it is listed under the phrase without comment. (6) The Peshitta’s New Testament writes מָריָא of God in Psa 110:1 but also of Jesus (Act 2:36; 1Co 8:6), so nothing is built on that form beyond the two forms in the quotation itself.

Left out: the personal names (names/adonijah, adoni-zedek, adoni-bezek, adoniram, adonikam); the places אַדָּן (Ezr 2:59, a.be.ad) and אַדּוֹן (Neh 7:61, a.be.ae); the redirect a.bf.ai; טוֹב אֲדוֹנִיָּה (2Ch 17:8), filed elsewhere. נְבוּזַרְאֲדָן and בַּלְאֲדָן contain these letters but are Babylonian names, not of this root.

No Aramaic word: Biblical Aramaic says מָרֵא (Dan 2:47; 4:16, 21; 5:23) and the Peshitta מָרָא / מָריָא, of root מרא, which has no entry yet; when it does, the two should point to each other.

Leads not followed: (a) no cognate for אֶדֶן “base”. Fisher 1969 (in his item on a Tigre word for “bottom”) mentions an Epigraphic South Arabian ʾdn “lower part” and a Tigre noun for the lower slope of a mountain; the OCR is too poor to cite, and Biella’s ʾDN has only “permit, authority; mind; clients” (p. 6), from the ear-word. Check Fisher’s PDF and Littmann-Höfner. Jastrow has אֶדֶן in later Hebrew (“base, pedestal”) and refers it to אוּדְנָא III; that entry was not found in the vendored file. (b) Akkadian has no lord-word of this shape in the Oracc glossaries (adannu is “fixed time”); Amorite names in ‑aduna were not checked. (c) Wiktionary lists Aramaic and Jewish Palestinian Aramaic אדונה; not verified in CAL. (d) Ἄδωνις, the Greek name of the Phoenician god, is a loan of ʾdn (Krahmalkov p. 34 under ʾDNY) but is not a New Testament word, so it is not recorded.
